rationale_summary: The document primarily frames AI governance as a matter of ensuring trustworthy, safe, and reliable AI systems that do not harm individuals or society. Core language centers on managing adverse impacts, ensuring accuracy, safety, privacy, and mitigating harmful bias for end users and communities. Innovation enablement is a secondary frame, as the document argues that managing risk builds trust and enables broader AI adoption. Fundamental rights and social stability appear as additional concerns via references to civil liberties, fairness, equity, and societal risk.

evidence_spans.quote: Ensuring that these inferences are helpful and not harmful in particular use cases – especially when inferences are rapidly scaled and amplified – is fundamental to trustworthy AI.

key characteristics which support trustworthiness, including accuracy, explainability and interpretability, privacy, reliability, robustness, safety, security (resilience) and mitigation of harmful bias
Cultivating trust and communication about how to understand and manage the risks of AI systems will help create opportunities for innovation and realize the full potential of this technology.
Their actions can designate boundaries for operation (technical or legal) and balance societal values and priorities related to civil liberties and rights, the economy, and security.
Identifying, mitigating, and minimizing risks and potential harms associated with AI technologies are essential steps towards the acceptance and widespread use of AI technologies.
